newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest dam flows may be reduced for fish.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest dam flows may be reduced for fish.

text.p: The Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) may need to cut daytime Northwest hydroelectric dam flows due to upcoming fish spawning requirements, regional industry sources said.
Under so-called "Vernita Bar" requirements, the volume of daytime flow on the Columbia River from October 15 to just before Thanksgiving sets the benchmark for minimum flows until early spring.
The requirements are aimed at making sure fish nests are built at a level which stays underwater for the winter.

Perry Gruber, a spokesman for BPA, said flows will be kept to between 50 and 70 kcfs (thousand cubic feet per second) at the rapids above the Vernita Bar site, effectively reducing flows at dams from Grand Coulee to John Day.
The idea is to set flows low enough so they can still be met if it is a dry water year, but high enough to prevent the fish nests from drying out, he added.
Some sources suggested that BPA may have been holding back on flows from the Grand Coulee dam, the first U.S. project on the Columbia, ahead of the Vernita Bar period.
The Federal power marketing agency also has some flexibility to cut back on Grand Coulee flows by adjusting from upstream reservoirs in Canada.
In addition, the Vernita Bar requirements can result in "negative load factoring," when daytime dam flows are diverted to nighttime hours.

"If the flow target is 50 kcfs (thousand cubic feet per second), but there are 100 kcfs in the sytem, you might have to run 150 kcfs at night in order to get to your daytime target," explained a spokesman for the U.S. Army Corp of Engineers, which operates federal dams in the Northwest.
A trade source at BPA said, "Typically we would hold flows down, but this year we will probably keep where we are. If it's a wet November we might have to hold some back."
